title: The Sulfur Town to the Airport Terminal: Lercara Friddi, the Commission, Havana, and the Long Naples Exile
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Lercara Friddi to the Lower East Side

stops.name: Lercara Friddi: the sulfur town, the birth
stops.date_confidence: Year attested and stable across every source consulted (en.wikipedia, Mob Museum, Britannica-derived chronologies). The day, 24 November, rests on the biographical tradition; no parish register has been seen for this file.
stops.campa: In a sulfur-mining town of the Sicilian interior, Antonio Lucania and Rosalia Caffarella name their third child Salvatore. Four others share the house: Giuseppe, Bartolomeo, Filippa, Concetta. The mine works give Lercara Friddi its economy and its dust, and the parish register gives the boy the only trace he leaves here. No plaque marks the door. He never comes back. The register entry stays where it is, and the name the town is known by afterwards is made on the other side of the Atlantic.
suggested_refs: The parish register of Lercara Friddi, the only documentary trace of the birth
The sulfur mine works that gave the town its economy in the 1890s
sources: The Mob Museum, Luciano biography pages

stops.name: Port of Palermo: the crossing west
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 1906 emigration is attested by en.wikipedia; History.com instead puts the family's arrival at his age ten, i.e. roughly 1907, and the two are not reconciled here. No ship manifest naming a port of embarkation has surfaced, so Palermo is the biographers' working assumption rather than a document. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: The Lucania family sails for New York in the great Sicilian emigration, one household among the hundreds of thousands leaving the island that decade. No manifest naming the port of embarkation has surfaced; Palermo is where the biographers put them, on the reasoning that a family from the interior would reach the sea by the capital rather than by a smaller harbor. The boy is eight. His name is Salvatore Lucania when he boards, and it does not survive the crossing in that form.
suggested_refs: Ellis Island passenger manifests for Palermo sailings, 1906, not located for this file
sources: History.com, Lucky Luciano biography (gives the later date)

stops.name: Ellis Island: processed at eight
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the year by en.wikipedia ('In 1906, when Luciano was eight years old'), which also fixes the age at eight, not nine. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Salvatore Lucania is processed here at eight years old, one entry among the millions the island logs in that decade, and passes into the city without ceremony. The harbor takes him back forty years later: in February 1946 he is held on this same island, a deported alien waiting for a berth, while the government that admitted the child arranges the removal of the man. He sails from Brooklyn, not from here. The island records him twice, forty years apart, once as an arrival and once as a removal.
suggested_refs: The Ellis Island registry room, processing point in 1906 and detention point in February 1946

stops.name: Cherry Street, Lower East Side: the tenement block
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction for the address. The Lower East Side settlement is attested; the specific building is not fixed in any reachable source. Standing gap.
stops.campa: The family settles into the tenement blocks north of the East River docks, where the Sicilian, Neapolitan, and Jewish streets run into one another within a few hundred yards. Here the boy anglicizes himself into Charlie Luciano, quits school at fourteen for a job delivering hats, and finds the block already organized by gangs that recruit from doorways. No reachable record fixes which of these buildings held the family, and the gap is left open here. The block itself is documented street by street.
suggested_refs: Lower East Side tenement house records, 1906-1920, address unidentified
sources: Tim Newark, Lucky Luciano: The Real and the Fake Gangster

stops.name: Five Points: twenty-five arrests and no cell
stops.date_confidence: Attested. History.com dates his standing in the Five Points milieu to 1916; en.wikipedia gives the 1916-1936 arrest count verbatim. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He is a leading man in the milieu around the remnants of the Five Points Gang, the same recruiting ground that sent Al Capone west to Chicago. Between 1916 and 1936 he is arrested twenty-five times on charges including assault, illegal gambling, blackmail, and robbery, and spends no time in prison for any of them. The twenty-five entries stand in the file as arrests and nothing further. Whatever the police collect in these years, the courts do not keep it.
suggested_refs: New York Police Department arrest records, 1916-1936, twenty-five entries

stops.name: New Hampton Farms, Orange County: the six months
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a live disagreement. The standard biographies (Sifakis, Newark) give a June 1916 heroin conviction and six months at the New Hampton Farms reformatory. En.wikipedia carries no such conviction and states he spent no prison time between 1916 and 1936. An earlier draft placed this at the Blackwell's Island penitentiary, which no reachable source supports.
stops.campa: The one custodial term the biographies give him before Dewey: a heroin conviction in June, six months at a reformatory farm in Orange County, well up the Hudson from the block that raised him. The accessible encyclopedia entry does not carry this sentence at all, and states plainly that he served no prison time between 1916 and 1936. Two reachable accounts, one silence and one six months. The pin stays where the biographies put it, and the disagreement stays with it.
suggested_refs: New York State reformatory records, New Hampton Farms, 1916, not consulted for this file
sources: Carl Sifakis, The Mafia Encyclopedia (at second hand)
Tim Newark, Lucky Luciano (at second hand)

stops.name: Delancey Street, Lower East Side: the boy who would not pay
stops.date_confidence: Pin and date inherited byte-identical from meyer_lansky.journey.json, which dates the encounter 1918. En.wikipedia places it earlier, in the school years, i.e. roughly 1911-1915. The two datings are not reconciled; the corpus pin is kept for continuity and the spread is recorded here.
stops.campa: Luciano runs a boy's protection racket on the walk home from school, charging the younger Jewish boys a penny or two a day for passage. One of them refuses to pay and offers to fight instead. His name is Meyer Lansky, and the refusal becomes a partnership that outlasts every other alliance either man makes. They meet here first, on this corner, and will meet again in Atlantic City, on the New York waterfront, and at the Hotel Nacional in Havana.
suggested_refs: meyer_lansky.journey.json, the Delancey and Lower East Side stop

segments.name: The Job, the Dice, the Gun

stops.name: Midtown Manhattan: the gambler's method
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the Masseria recruitment and the Rothstein employment (en.wikipedia). The pin is inherited from meyer_lansky.journey.json, which fixes Rothstein's 1928 murder in Midtown. The often-repeated 'partnership with Rothstein' is not supported: the source says Luciano and his associates worked for him.
stops.campa: Joe Masseria, boss of lower Manhattan, recruits him as a gunman. In the same years he and his close associates start working for Arnold Rothstein, the gambler who runs the underworld as a ledger business with an insulated principal and no fingerprints on anything. Prohibition supplies the product; Rothstein supplies the method. In 1928 Rothstein is shot in this district and dies, and the men who worked under him keep the method. Twenty years on it is running the casinos in Havana.
suggested_refs: meyer_lansky.journey.json, the Rothstein murder stop, Midtown Manhattan 1928

stops.name: Barbizon-Plaza Hotel: the alias Charles Lane
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the hotel, the alias, and the 1927 lieutenancy (en.wikipedia; History.com). The income figures are attested for 1925 and are carried as the source gives them: over twelve million gross, about four million personal, not four million gross. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He keeps rooms on Central Park South under the name Charles Lane, a few blocks from the park, well dressed and unremarkable. By 1925 he is grossing over twelve million dollars a year and keeping about four million of it after the payoffs. A 1923 arrest for selling heroin has damaged his standing, and he repairs it by being seen in the right rooms with the right people. The same year Masseria makes him his top lieutenant. By 1927 the name on the hotel register is Charles Lane's and the payroll is Masseria's.
suggested_refs: The Barbizon-Plaza Hotel register under the name Charles Lane

stops.name: Atlantic City: the conference that draws the map
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Pin and date inherited byte-identical from meyer_lansky.journey.json, which dates the conference 13-16 May 1929 at the Ritz-Carlton and Ambassador hotels.
stops.campa: For four days in May, Lansky, Luciano, Johnny Torrio, and Frank Costello sit in the Ritz-Carlton and the Ambassador and divide the country: territories agreed, arbitration in place of shooting, a syndicate answering to a table rather than to a man. The arrangement is drawn two years before the war that will make it stick, the war between Masseria and Maranzano still to come. Lansky works the same four days from the accountant's chair, Luciano from the muscle's end, two views of one table.
suggested_refs: meyer_lansky.journey.json, the Atlantic City Conference stop

stops.name: Staten Island: the beam in the warehouse
stops.date_confidence: Month attested, day unknown and defaulted. En.wikipedia gives only 'In October 1929' and describes a warehouse on Staten Island, not a beach. An earlier draft supplied 16 October, the Huguenot district, and a shoreline; all three are reconstruction and the shoreline is dropped. The coordinates locate Staten Island, not the building.
stops.campa: Three men force him into a limousine at gunpoint, beat and stab him, and hang him by the hands from a beam in a warehouse on Staten Island. He lives. He gives the police a name and never repeats it afterward. The newspapers make the survival the origin of the nickname, though he never confirms that reading; other accounts trace Lucky to a run of gambling fortune, or to nothing more than an American tongue failing at Lucania. The scar on his face settles the question for the photographers.
suggested_refs: Contemporary New York press accounts of the October 1929 abduction, not located in full for this file

stops.name: New York: the war opens with Reina
stops.date_confidence: Attested. En.wikipedia 'Castellammarese War' dates the war 26 February 1930 to 15 April 1931 and states that Masseria ordered the Reina killing. History.com's 'in 1928 a feud broke out' is an outlier and is not followed. The attribution of the Reina murder to Luciano, which circulates widely, is supported by no source checked.
stops.campa: Masseria orders the killing of his own ally Gaetano Reina, and the Castellammarese War begins between Masseria's people and Salvatore Maranzano's. It runs fourteen months and kills men on both sides while Luciano, Masseria's lieutenant, calculates which boss he needs less. The order for Reina is Masseria's, not his; the popular account that hands Luciano the trigger here is not supported by any source consulted. He spends it as a lieutenant, taking orders from one of the two men fighting it.
suggested_refs: English Wikipedia, 'Castellammarese War', infobox dating 26 February 1930 to 15 April 1931

stops.name: Nuova Villa Tammaro, Coney Island: the long lunch
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the date and the restaurant (en.wikipedia, 'Lucky Luciano' and 'Giuseppe Masseria'). The exact street address of the restaurant is not confirmed in any reachable source. Who fired is attributed differently across accounts; Luciano's foreknowledge is not seriously disputed.
stops.campa: Luciano and his boss take a long lunch at the Nuova Villa Tammaro, cards after the food, the restaurant emptied of witnesses by the hour. Luciano excuses himself to the restroom. Masseria is shot dead at the table before he returns. Who fires is attributed differently by every account; that Luciano knew is disputed by almost nobody. The war ends at Masseria's own lunch table, and the street address of the restaurant has never surfaced in any account.
suggested_refs: Press photographs of the Nuova Villa Tammaro interior, 15 April 1931

stops.name: New York Central Building, Park Avenue: the false tax agents
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia, 'Salvatore Maranzano' and 'Lucky Luciano'). The building is now the Helmsley Building at 230 Park Avenue.
stops.campa: Maranzano, having declared himself boss of bosses over the reorganized families, keeps his office in the New York Central Building above Grand Central. Four men enter with badges, saying they are tax agents, and stab and shoot him at his desk. The contract Maranzano had placed on Luciano's own life is days from being filled. Both claimants to the top are dead inside five months, and Luciano is in neither room when it happens. He inherits the settlement without a charge attached to either killing.
suggested_refs: The New York Central Building, 230 Park Avenue, now the Helmsley Building

stops.name: Waldorf Astoria: the suite and the Commission
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Waldorf suite under the name Charles Ross rests on the biographies (Raab, Newark), not on a document seen here. The 1931 founding of the Commission is reported by en.wikipedia and History.com, with an organizing meeting placed in Chicago, but venue, date, and roster vary enough across the reachable sources that the month here is chosen, not attested.
stops.campa: He takes a suite under the name Charles Ross and runs the business from a hotel rather than a headquarters, on the reasoning that a boss with no fixed office is harder to tie to a conspiracy. In the same season the Commission is set up: five New York families and the out-of-town bosses, a standing body with arbitration in place of a throne. The founding meeting's venue, date, and roster are reported loosely enough across the sources that only the structure is settled; the ceremony itself stays undocumented.
suggested_refs: Selwyn Raab, Five Families, on the Commission's founding structure

stops.name: New York: two hundred doors in one night
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): roughly two hundred brothels raided, sixteen men and eighty-seven women arrested. Dewey was a United States Attorney appointed special prosecutor by Governor Herbert Lehman in June 1935, not a District Attorney; Eunice Carter was Dewey's assistant district attorney and led the investigation.
stops.campa: On a single night some two hundred brothels are raided across the city; sixteen men and eighty-seven women are taken in. The investigation that built the map is led by Eunice Carter, assistant district attorney under the special prosecutor Thomas Dewey, whom Governor Herbert Lehman appointed the previous June. Carter works the one racket a boss cannot insulate himself from, because the women who run it can be arrested and asked questions. The women become the case.
suggested_refs: The February 1936 vice raid arrest dockets, New York County

stops.name: Hot Springs, Arkansas: the tolerant sheriff
stops.date_confidence: Arrest date attested (en.wikipedia): 3 April 1936, ninety counts of compulsory prostitution. That he was warned of the coming indictment is reconstruction. The hotel or house that lodged him in Hot Springs is not fixed in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Warned of the indictment, he goes to the Arkansas spa town that keeps a standing arrangement with wanted men and a sheriff disinclined to look. He is arrested there on ninety counts of compulsory prostitution and fights extradition from a cell in a resort. The fight is lost and he is returned to New York under guard. Which hotel or house sheltered him in Hot Springs is not recorded in anything reachable, which is roughly the condition the town was selling to men in his position.
suggested_refs: Garland County, Arkansas extradition proceedings, spring 1936

stops.name: Criminal Courts Building, Centre Street: the chain-store testimony
stops.date_confidence: Trial opening and the 7 June conviction on sixty-two counts are attested (en.wikipedia). The venue is corrected: the Court of General Sessions before Judge Philip J. McCook sat in the Criminal Courts Building on Centre Street, not at 60 Centre Street, which housed the civil and appellate terms. The coordinates for the old Criminal Courts Building are approximate.
stops.campa: Dewey prosecutes in person before Judge Philip McCook in the Court of General Sessions. The witnesses are the madams and the women taken in February, and they testify to what Luciano said in front of them about the business: that it should be organized the way a chain of grocery stores is organized. On 7 June the jury convicts on sixty-two counts of compulsory prostitution. No source reachable here has seen the transcript; the words survive through a historian who quotes it.
stops.quote: the same as the A&P stores are, a large syndicate ... the same as chain stores ... [g]o ahead and crack the joint
stops.quote_source: Witness testimony in People v. Luciano (New York, 1936), quoted in Robert Weldon Whalen, Murder, Inc., and the Moral Life: Gangsters and Gangbusters in La Guardia's New York (Fordham University Press, 2016), p. 114, as cited on the English Wikipedia article 'Lucky Luciano'. Secondhand report of Luciano's speech by a prosecution witness, not his own courtroom statement. Whalen p. 114 could not be opened for this file (Google Books HTTP 429).
suggested_refs: The People v. Luciano trial record, New York County Court of General Sessions, 1936, not located in full text
sources: Robert Weldon Whalen, Murder, Inc., and the Moral Life (2016), p. 114, at second hand

stops.name: Criminal Courts Building, Centre Street: thirty to fifty years
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): sentence of thirty to fifty years handed down 18 June 1936, described as the longest for the charge in the state's history.
stops.campa: McCook sentences him to thirty to fifty years, the longest term the state has handed down for the charge. Dewey's career is made on the verdict and will carry him to the governorship of New York, from which he will one day sign the paper that lets this prisoner out. Luciano is thirty-eight. He will run the Commission from inside for nearly ten years, through visitors and lawyers who carry instructions back to the city, until a war finds a use for a convicted man.
suggested_refs: The sentencing minutes of Judge Philip J. McCook, 18 June 1936

stops.name: Sing Sing, Ossining: the intake
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Sing Sing was the first place of imprisonment and that the move to Clinton came 'later in 1936' (en.wikipedia). The month here is reconstruction; no reception date has been seen. An earlier draft omitted Sing Sing entirely.
stops.campa: He is received into the state system at Ossining, the intake point for New York felons, and processed like any of them: number, photograph, prison clothing, a cell above the river. The stay is short. The state has no intention of keeping the most famous prisoner it owns within an hour of the city that convicted him and within reach of men who still take his instructions. A transfer order is written before the year is out, and the destination is near the Canadian line.
suggested_refs: Sing Sing reception records, 1936, not consulted for this file

stops.name: Clinton Correctional Facility, Dannemora: Little Siberia
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the transfer happened 'later in 1936' (en.wikipedia); the month is reconstruction. Coordinates corrected to en.wikipedia 'Clinton Correctional Facility' (44 deg 43 min 25 sec N, 73 deg 43 min 15 sec W); an earlier draft used -73.7476, about two kilometres west into open country.
stops.campa: Clinton Correctional Facility sits near the Canadian border, and the inmates call it Little Siberia for the cold and the distance. He serves the bulk of the sentence here. Visitors come the whole way up: lawyers, family, men from the Commission carrying questions and taking answers back. In 1942 a different kind of visitor arrives, with a naval commission and a problem on the New York waterfront, and the sentence he is serving is the only thing either side has to trade.
suggested_refs: Clinton Correctional Facility inmate records, 1936-1942

stops.name: 90 Church Street: the Third Naval District
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. That the New York liaison was run from the Third Naval District and worked through Lansky is attested; the precise offices and meeting rooms are not detailed in anything reachable. Month and day chosen to place the stop in early 1942, when the waterfront problem was acute.
stops.campa: The Third Naval District runs its intelligence work from lower Manhattan, and with ships burning off the coast it needs the New York piers quiet. The official channel is the longshoremen's union. The working channel is Meyer Lansky, who carries the Navy's question inland to a prison and brings the answer back. Which rooms in which building held the meetings is not detailed in anything reachable; that the operation was run from this district, and run through Lansky, is.
suggested_refs: Rodney Campbell, The Luciano Project, on the Third Naval District liaison
meyer_lansky.journey.json, the Operation Underworld stop
sources: Rodney Campbell, The Luciano Project (at second hand)

stops.name: Great Meadow, Comstock: the lawyer and the accountant
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the transfer and the visits by Moses Polakoff and Meyer Lansky; the month is reconstruction. Coordinates corrected to en.wikipedia 'Great Meadow Correctional Facility' (43 deg 27 min 27 sec N, 73 deg 25 min 59 sec W); an earlier draft placed the pin about thirteen kilometres south-east of Comstock.
stops.campa: He is moved to Comstock, in Washington County, where visits are easier to arrange. His lawyer Moses Polakoff and Meyer Lansky come and go, and the bargain takes shape: labour peace on the docks against sabotage, and later contacts among Sicilian mafiosi held to be useful to the invasion of Sicily. Benito Mussolini's regime had spent the 1920s crushing that same mafia with a prefect's free hand. In July 1943 the landings that break the regime come ashore where those men live.
suggested_refs: mussolini.journey.json, the 1943 Sicilian landings and the fall of the regime
sources: Rodney Campbell, The Luciano Project (at second hand)

stops.name: Albany: the prosecutor signs the release
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): commutation by Governor Thomas Dewey on 3 January 1946, conditional on deportation. The wartime justification is contested at its own source: en.wikipedia 'Operation Underworld' documents the labour-peace cooperation with Commander Charles Haffenden but records that no Axis agent was ever tied to the loss of the Normandie and that postwar Axis records claim no such operation existed.
stops.campa: Thomas Dewey, now governor of New York, commutes the sentence of the man he convicted, on the single condition that he leave the country and not return. The wartime service is the stated ground. Historians will find the labour-peace cooperation with Commander Charles Haffenden documented and the sabotage-prevention story unproven: no Axis agent was ever tied to the loss of the Normandie, and postwar Axis records claim no such operation existed. The commutation is real regardless.
suggested_refs: The executive clemency file, State of New York, 3 January 1946

stops.name: Ellis Island: the alien of the Kingdom of Italy
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): transported to Ellis Island on 2 February 1946 to begin deportation proceedings. He was held at the island but sailed from a Brooklyn pier eight days later, so no embarkation happened here.
stops.campa: He is brought to the island to begin deportation proceedings, forty years after passing through it in the other direction as a child of eight. The papers name him an alien of the Kingdom of Italy, which is what he has been the whole time; he never took citizenship, and without it there is nothing for a lawyer to argue. Nine days of formalities, then a car to Brooklyn. The conviction took Dewey a special prosecutor's office and a year of witnesses; the deportation takes a birth certificate.
suggested_refs: Immigration and Naturalization Service deportation file, February 1946

stops.name: Bush Terminal, Brooklyn: the ship whose name is not certain
stops.date_confidence: Date attested; pier and vessel are reconstruction. En.wikipedia says only 'On February 10, Luciano's ship sailed from Brooklyn for Italy', naming neither. The Bush Terminal pin and the vessel name Laura Keene circulate in secondary accounts and are not confirmed by anything reachable here. An earlier draft tagged this attested.
stops.campa: His ship sails from Brooklyn for Italy on 10 February 1946. Longshoremen line the pier, and the accounts of the send-off do not agree on the vessel; the name Laura Keene circulates in the secondary literature without confirmation, and the pier itself is a reconstruction. What is attested is the date and the direction. He has served nine and a half years of the thirty-to-fifty-year sentence, and he leaves the country that convicted him with a governor's signature in his file and no right of return.
suggested_refs: Port of New York sailing records, 10 February 1946, vessel unidentified

stops.name: Port of Naples: seventeen days out of Brooklyn
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): 'On February 28, after a 17-day voyage, the ship arrived in Naples.' An earlier draft presented a rival Genoa landfall for 1946 as a live source discrepancy; no source checked does this. Genoa is the April 1947 arrival from Cuba, and the two voyages were being collided.
stops.campa: Seventeen days out of Brooklyn, the ship puts in at Naples, and he steps ashore in a country he left at eight and cannot remember. Italian journalists are waiting; American ones will come. He is a national curiosity in a bombed-out port city where the black market is the economy and the Allied Military Government is still counting things. He speaks the language badly. He will die in this city sixteen years from now, four kilometres from where he lands.
suggested_refs: Italian press coverage of the Naples landing, 28 February 1946

stops.name: Camaguey: the inland door into Cuba
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): secret relocation to Cuba on 29 October 1946 by way of Venezuela and Brazil, entering through Camaguey rather than Havana. The Miramar residence in Havana is reconstruction and is not given a separate pin here.
stops.campa: He flies into Cuba by an inland city rather than by Havana, having crossed through Venezuela and Brazil to arrive without a customs officer at the capital noticing. Eight months of exile have been enough. Cuba is ninety miles from Florida and outside American jurisdiction, and Fulgencio Batista's Havana already runs on a casino arrangement Meyer Lansky manages from the American side. From Camaguey he goes west to the capital and takes a house in the walled suburb of Miramar.
suggested_refs: meyer_lansky.journey.json, the Havana casino-protection stops under Batista

stops.name: Hotel Nacional de Cuba, Havana: the conference convenes
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia 'Havana Conference'): 'The Havana Conference convened on December 20, 1946', held during the week of 22 December and running a little more than a week. An earlier draft used 22 December as the opening date. Pin inherited byte-identical from meyer_lansky.journey.json; it agrees to four decimals with the coordinates on en.wikipedia 'Hotel Nacional de Cuba'.
stops.campa: The conference convenes on Taganana Hill above the harbour and runs a little more than a week. New York and New Jersey, Chicago, Buffalo, New Orleans, and Tampa send their bosses; the Jewish Syndicate sends its men; Frank Sinatra sings in the cabaret and gives the week its cover story. The agenda is narcotics routes, Cuban gambling, and the cost overruns on Benjamin Siegel's Flamingo in the Nevada desert. The room votes to have Siegel killed and postpones it until the hotel opens.
suggested_refs: meyer_lansky.journey.json, the Havana Conference stop
English Wikipedia, 'Havana Conference'

stops.name: Havana: the answer to Vito Genovese
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction for the day; the meeting is placed within the conference week of December 1946. Pin inherited byte-identical from meyer_lansky.journey.json's general Havana coordinate. The wording of the reply has been checked verbatim against the English Wikipedia article; the book it cites could not be opened this session.
stops.campa: Vito Genovese comes to his suite privately and proposes that Luciano take the title of boss of bosses and let Genovese run the daily business underneath it. Luciano has already refused the title in front of the full conference, and refuses it again here. The reply is preserved by a historian of the Cuban years, not by any transcript, and no primary text has been opened: the wording has been checked against the article that carries it, and the book behind that article could not be reached this session.
stops.quote: There is no Boss of Bosses. I turned it down in front of everybody. If I ever change my mind, I will take the title. But it won't be up to you. Right now, you work for me, and I ain't in the mood to retire. Don't you ever let me hear this again, or I'll lose my temper.
stops.quote_source: T. J. English, Havana Nocturne: How the Mob Owned Cuba - and Then Lost It to the Revolution (Harper, 2008), p. 28, as cited on the English Wikipedia article 'Lucky Luciano'. Verified verbatim against the article's raw wikitext; English p. 28 itself could not be opened (Google Books HTTP 429, Archive.org full-text unreachable). Frequently misattributed to Gosch and Hammer; that attribution is not the one the article carries.
suggested_refs: T. J. English, Havana Nocturne (Harper, 2008), p. 28
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Lucky Luciano' (raw wikitext, footnote target verified)
T. J. English, Havana Nocturne (2008), at second hand

stops.name: Vedado, Havana: the casino district
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Lansky's management role in the Havana casinos under Batista's licensing is documented; Luciano's personal ownership stake is asserted more firmly in popular accounts than in any record reachable here. Cuban casino licensing records for 1946-1958 were not accessible for this research.
stops.campa: The casino circuit runs through this district: the Nacional, the Montmartre, the licences Batista signs and the American capital that fills them. Lansky manages, and Luciano is understood to hold a stake, though popular accounts assert his personal ownership more firmly than any licensing record has confirmed. Six days after the conference closes, the Flamingo opens in Las Vegas. Twelve years on, Che Guevara's column will come down out of Santa Clara and close this street's business in a week.
suggested_refs: che_guevara.journey.json, the entry into Havana, January 1959
Cuban casino licensing records, 1946-1958, not accessible
sources: Popular Havana Conference and Lansky-network accounts

stops.name: Port of Havana: the medicine held back
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): Anslinger's pressure on 21 February 1947, the Cuban announcement of deportation within forty-eight hours on 23 February. The vessel that carried him out is inconsistently reported across secondary sources and is not named here.
stops.campa: Harry Anslinger, the United States narcotics commissioner, tells Cuba that American pharmaceutical shipments will stop until Luciano is gone. Two days later the Cuban government announces his deportation within forty-eight hours. He is put aboard a freighter here, and the secondary accounts disagree about which one. The Cuban refuge has lasted under four months. The arrangement he came to bless survives him on the island another twelve years, and outlives the government that expelled him by weeks.
suggested_refs: United States Federal Bureau of Narcotics correspondence with Cuba, February 1947

stops.name: Port of Genoa: arrested on the gangway
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): arrest at Genoa on 11 April 1947. An earlier draft asserted a documented transfer from Genoa into custody in Sicily; the source does not describe the Palermo detention as the immediate consequence of this arrest, and the two are kept separate here.
stops.campa: Italian police arrest him at the quay as he lands on 11 April 1947, under the terms of the deportation status he broke by leaving Italy for Cuba. He has now been expelled from the United States and from Cuba inside fourteen months, and the country obliged to take him does not want him either. What follows the Genoa arrest is Italian custody in general. The Palermo detention is a separate matter, later, and no source describes a transfer from this quay to that particular cell.
suggested_refs: Italian police records of the Genoa arrest, 11 April 1947

stops.name: Ucciardone Prison, Palermo: a month and no charge
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he was briefly held at Palermo after the expulsion from Cuba and released for want of grounds; the month is reconstruction and the day is defaulted. Coordinates corrected to it.wikipedia 'Carcere dell'Ucciardone' (38 deg 07 min 58 sec N, 13 deg 21 min 28 sec E, Via Enrico Albanese 3), about four kilometres east of an earlier draft's pin.
stops.campa: He is held in the Bourbon prison by the Palermo waterfront while the Italian authorities look for a law he has broken on their own soil and find none that will hold. A month, and he is released without charge. He is fifty, back on the island his family left in 1906, a prisoner in it for four weeks and a resident of it by order thereafter. He is arrested again in Rome two years later, so this is not the last cell he sees, whatever the later summaries say.
suggested_refs: Carcere dell'Ucciardone, Via Enrico Albanese 3, Palermo

stops.name: Via Tasso, Naples: the appliance shop
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the street and the shop (it.wikipedia: he 'si trasferi definitivamente in via Tasso' and opened 'un negozio di elettrodomestici ed articoli sanitari'). Two earlier drafts placed the residence in Posillipo and on Via Tasso, four kilometres apart; the sourced address wins. Coordinates here follow the run of Via Tasso itself, since both earlier pins missed it. The house number is not in any source.
stops.campa: He settles for good on a street climbing the hill west of the Corso Vittorio Emanuele, and opens a shop selling household appliances and sanitary goods. Igea Lissoni, a Milanese ballerina twenty years younger, comes to live with him; they never marry. Italian and American police maintain through every one of these years that the shop is a cover and the income is heroin. No source gives the house number. The shop stays open for the fourteen years he has left, and the police file grows beside it.
suggested_refs: Via Tasso, Naples; the appliance and sanitary-goods shop, address unrecorded

stops.name: Excelsior Hotel, Via Veneto, Rome: photographed and released
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the Roman visibility in 1948 and for the July 1949 arrest on suspicion of narcotics trafficking followed by release without charges (en.wikipedia). Month and day of the 1948 sighting are reconstruction.
stops.campa: Photographers find him on the Via Veneto, heavier, well tailored, entirely visible, and the pictures run in two countries as proof that exile has cost him nothing he minds. In July 1949 Rome police arrest him on suspicion of narcotics trafficking and release him within days with no charge that will stand. It sets the pattern for the Italian years. He is watched without interruption and prosecuted for nothing, and the photographers reach him more often than the police do.
suggested_refs: Italian press photographs of Luciano on the Via Veneto, 1948

stops.name: Naples Questura: the interrogation that goes nowhere
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 9 June 1951 questioning rests on summary accounts rather than on any Italian police document seen for this file. The 1952 revocation of his passport is separately attested by en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Naples police bring him in for questioning, one of a series of interviews conducted under American pressure and Italian obligation. Nothing chargeable comes of it, as nothing chargeable comes of any of them, and the questioning resumes at intervals for the rest of his life. In 1952 the Italian government revokes his passport, which ends the question of where else he might go. He is fifty-three, in a country he did not choose and can no longer leave.
suggested_refs: Questura di Napoli files on Salvatore Lucania, 1948-1962, not consulted

stops.name: Naples: the soggiorno obbligato
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 1 November 1954 restriction order rests on summary accounts, not on the commission's own record. Pin inherited byte-identical from the corpus's canonical Naples coordinate, used in the queue entry framing the planned Italian branch of this cluster.
stops.campa: A public-security commission formally restricts him to residence in Naples, the measure Italian law reserves for men it considers mafiosi and cannot convict. He is required to stay in the city and to be findable in it. The restriction holds for the rest of his life. He is fifty-seven, cannot leave Italy, cannot leave Naples, and receives American journalists at a cafe table, where he talks freely: there is nowhere further to send him and no charge outstanding to be careful about.
suggested_refs: The public-security commission order of 1 November 1954, not consulted

stops.name: Grand Hotel et des Palmes, Palermo: the disputed summit
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, both lenses. History.com asserts that Luciano convened a meeting of Italian and American mafiosi in Palermo in 1957; that men met in October 1957 at this hotel is widely reported, but its status as one formal summit with an agreed agenda, and Luciano's role in convening it, are disputed among historians of the period. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: Tradition places a meeting of Sicilian and American mafiosi in this belle-epoque hotel, Luciano among them, remembered since as the summit that opened the heroin route from Sicily to New York. That men met is well attested. That it was one formal summit with an agreed agenda, convened by Luciano, is disputed by historians who read the week as a looser set of conversations later compressed into a single legend. Both readings stand, and neither is settled here.
suggested_refs: The Grand Hotel et des Palmes, Palermo, October 1957
sources: Journalistic and popular accounts of the 1957 Palermo conference; formal-summit framing contested

stops.name: Naples: the death of Igea Lissoni
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (en.wikipedia): Igea Lissoni died of breast cancer in 1959. Month and day unknown, defaulted. The quote's wording is verified verbatim against the English Wikipedia article; the book cited could not be opened this session.
stops.campa: Igea Lissoni dies of breast cancer, eleven years after coming south to live with him. He has no children by her or by anyone, and when he is asked why, the answer he gives is about the name rather than about the woman. The same winter, in the city he made his last headquarters before Naples, Batista flies out of Camp Columbia and Fidel Castro's people come in, and the Havana arrangement he convened the 1946 conference to protect ends inside a fortnight.
stops.quote: I didn't want no son of mine to go through life as the son of Luciano, the gangster. That's one thing I still hate Dewey for, making me a gangster in the eyes of the world.
stops.quote_source: Tim Newark, Lucky Luciano: The Real and the Fake Gangster (Thomas Dunne Books, 2010), p. 240, as cited on the English Wikipedia article 'Lucky Luciano'. Verified verbatim against the article's raw wikitext; Newark p. 240 itself could not be opened (Archive.org copy lending-restricted, Google Books HTTP 429). Frequently misattributed to Gosch and Hammer, which Newark is not.
suggested_refs: fidel_castro.journey.json, the Camp Columbia entry of 8 January 1959
Tim Newark, Lucky Luciano (2010), p. 240

stops.name: Capodichino Airport, Naples: the producer's appointment
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): heart attack at Naples airport on 26 January 1962, aged 64, while going to meet the producer Martin Gosch. Accounts differ on whether he was still alive when reached; that detail is reconstruction.
stops.campa: He drives to the airport to meet Martin Gosch, an American producer who wants to make a film of his life, and dies of a heart attack in the terminal at sixty-four. Accounts differ on whether anyone reached him breathing. The film is never made. Thirteen years later Gosch and Richard Hammer publish a book of what they say were his own words, and the New York Times reports before it appears that the text quotes him on events that happened after his death.
suggested_refs: Martin A. Gosch and Richard Hammer, The Last Testament of Lucky Luciano (Little, Brown, 1975), authenticity contested

stops.name: St. John Cemetery, Middle Village: the one crossing left
stops.date_confidence: Attested (en.wikipedia): burial at St. John Cemetery with more than 2,000 mourners and a eulogy by Carlo Gambino; the Naples funeral of 29 January with eight black plumed horses is from it.wikipedia. Day of burial unknown, defaulted. Coordinates corrected to en.wikipedia 'St. John Cemetery (Queens)'; an earlier draft carried a longitude with the minus sign dropped, placing the grave in the Bay of Bengal. Mausoleum, section, and inscription are not in any source: a Find a Grave check was blocked by HTTP 403.
stops.campa: Three days after the death, three hundred people follow a hearse drawn by eight black plumed horses through Naples to the church of Santissima Trinita. Then the United States government grants permission for the body, and he crosses the Atlantic a last time in a cargo hold, admitted dead to the country that deported him living. More than two thousand mourners come to Middle Village. Carlo Gambino gives the eulogy. The section and the inscription have never surfaced in any reachable source.
